case_study_insert.main_stem: Westline Logistics Xpress (WLX) is a public limited company in the warehousing and distribution sector, employing a workforce of 60. Founded in 2008 by Daniel Okafor, the business stores and distributes fast-moving consumer goods for retailers and operates a hierarchical structure with autocratic leadership. WLX plans to invest $900,000 in automated racking and computer stock control, financed by a $600,000 bank loan and a $300,000 share issue. It has fixed costs of $420,000 a year, a variable cost of $9.00 a unit and a selling price of $16.00, and currently handles 74,000 units a year. WLX faces two operational problems: stock damage has reached 3.6% of units handled and warehouse absenteeism is rising, causing complaints from retailers about inaccurate orders.
case_study_insert.appendix_1_marketing_ops: Operations and Quality Report — Q4 2025: The warehouse picked 18,600 orders last month with a damage rate of 3.6%, down from 5.2% a year earlier. Customer complaints fell from 72 to 41 per month. Average order fulfilment is 3.4 days. A survey of 450 retail managers found that 66% would pay up to $0.60 more for error-free fulfilment, and 62% check stock accuracy before renewing contracts. A training needs analysis shows 21 of 60 warehouse staff lack computer stock-control skills; on-the-job training is offered, while off-the-job training at the local college costs $880 per employee.

appendix_2_financial_data.title: Extract from the Statement of Profit or Loss and Capital employed data of Westline Logistics Xpress for the year ended 31 March 2025 ($ '000)

case_study_insert.appendix_3_external_environment: Economic and Business Bulletin (November 2026): (1) The central bank raised the base interest rate from 4.00% to 4.75%, raising borrowing costs on variable-rate loans. (2) The national minimum wage will rise by 6.0% from $13.00 to $13.78 per hour from April 2026, pushing up warehouse wage bills. (3) Energy and packaging input costs rose 10.5% year-on-year, retail sales grew 2.8%, and business rates for distribution centres increased 4.3%.

questions.question_text: WLX raised $300,000 through a share issue. Explain two advantages for WLX of funding part of the $900,000 automation project with a share issue rather than more bank debt.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: A share issue brings in $300,000 of permanent capital that never has to be repaid, so unlike the $600,000 bank loan it creates no monthly interest or principal burden. With fixed costs of $420,000 a year and retail sales growing only 2.8%, this protects WLX's cash flow while the automated racking is installed and the 3.6% stock-damage rate is tackled.

Point 2: Equity finance improves the company's debt profile, leaving more of the gross profit in the business rather than paying interest to a lender, and it does not require pledging assets as collateral. The $880 per employee training cost and the 10.5% rise in energy and packaging inputs can therefore be met from the $300,000 without risking the racking investment; existing shareholders accept some dilution, but as a public limited company WLX can access this source of finance readily. With 2024 revenue of $3,000,000 in Appendix 2, WLX has the scale to absorb the $300,000 of new equity.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation and analysis applied to WLX and its automation financing decision.

questions.question_text: WLX is promoting its new error-free fulfilment service to retailers. Consider a national television campaign, trade-magazine advertising, or direct partnerships with retail chains. Which should WLX choose to promote the service? Justify your recommendation.
questions.model_answer:
Television campaign: A national TV campaign would build quick, broad awareness of error-free fulfilment, but airtime and production costs are extremely high and almost no viewer is a retail procurement manager. For a 60-employee distributor already funding a $900,000 automation project and a $600,000 loan, the wasted spend would be very large and few of the 450 surveyed retail managers would be reached.

Trade-magazine advertising: Specialist logistics and retail publications are cheaper and reach industry professionals, so the message about cutting the 3.6% damage rate would land with relevant readers. However, reach is small and slow, and cannot alone persuade the 62% of managers who check stock accuracy before renewing contracts; it is a supporting channel rather than a decisive one.

Direct partnerships with retail chains: Working directly with the retailers WLX already serves targets exactly the 66% of 450 managers willing to pay $0.60 more for error-free fulfilment, with negotiated contracts and measurable service data. The $0.60 premium can be built into service-level agreements, and the 62% who check stock accuracy can be shown the improved figures from the new racking.

Recommendation: WLX should choose direct partnerships with retail chains. This reaches the precise decision-makers in the survey, costs far less than television and delivers contracted volume rather than vague brand awareness. Television is rejected as unaffordable and untargeted given the $600,000 loan; trade magazines are rejected as too narrow to win contracts on their own, though they can support the partnership approach. The 3.4-day fulfilment time can be quoted in the direct proposals to retailers as evidence of reliability.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Limited knowledge or outline of the promotional options with minimal context.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Detailed discussion of the advantages and disadvantages of at least two options in the context of WLX with some judgement.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed discussion of all three options in the context of WLX with a well-justified recommendation explaining why television and trade magazines are rejected.

questions.question_text: WLX's warehouse absenteeism is rising and its hierarchical structure with autocratic leadership is resented. Explain two benefits for WLX of introducing democratic leadership to reduce absenteeism.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Democratic leadership gives WLX's workforce of 60 a voice in how the new automated racking and computer stock-control systems are introduced, satisfying social and esteem needs and raising job satisfaction. Staff who help design picking routines and shifts are more likely to attend regularly, reducing the absenteeism that currently disrupts the 74,000-unit operation and the 3.6% damage problem.

Point 2: Consulting warehouse staff generates practical ideas for cutting the rising stock damage and inaccurate orders, since they handle the goods daily. Greater involvement increases commitment, lowers labour turnover and saves the $880 per employee retraining cost, protecting service quality as the $900,000 automation is installed. Higher morale also supports the stock accuracy that 62% of surveyed retail managers check before renewing contracts. The damage rate has already fallen from 5.2% to 3.6%, evidence that staff involvement can improve accuracy and support the 62% of managers who check stock records.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid benefit identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual development linked to WLX's absenteeism, quality and output.

questions.question_text: WLX must train 21 warehouse staff to operate the new computer stock-control systems. Consider on-the-job training or off-the-job training at the local college. Which should WLX choose? Justify your decision.
questions.model_answer:
On-the-job training: Training beside the new racking is directly relevant to WLX's own stock-control system, costs no course fees, and keeps the 21 staff productive while they learn, protecting the 74,000-unit operation and the effort to cut the 3.6% damage rate. However, trainers are working staff whose own picking suffers, bad habits can be passed on, and there is no formal certificate if retailers ask for evidence of competence.

Off-the-job training: A college course at $880 per employee gives structured, up-to-date computer skills and a recognised certificate for all 21, costing $18,480 in total — modest beside the $900,000 automation project. It removes staff from the warehouse, cutting short-term capacity, and generic content may not match WLX's exact system, so depot follow-up would still be needed.

Decision: WLX should choose on-the-job training for the initial rollout, backed by short college modules for senior staff. It is cheapest, system-specific and avoids further capacity loss while absenteeism is rising; full off-the-job training is rejected because paying $18,480 and releasing 21 staff would disrupt order fulfilment for retailers, and college visits can be added once the racking is running reliably and the 3.6% damage rate falls. With 18,600 orders picked last month, releasing 21 staff would slow fulfilment while complaints still run at 41 a month. On-the-job training protects the 74,000-unit operation, and the $18,480 saved could pay for certified short courses once the racking is stable and the 3.6% damage rate is lower. Senior staff can then coach the rest of the warehouse team, protecting the 3.4-day fulfilment time while the new racking beds in.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Basic description of the two training methods with limited application to WLX.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Detailed analysis of the benefits and drawbacks of one or both training methods in the context of WLX.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Comprehensive evaluation of both training methods in the context of WLX with a well-justified decision covering cost, disruption and relevance.

questions.question_text: Calculate and explain how WLX's management can use its cost, break-even and productivity data.

sub_parts.model_answer: Formula: Break-even output = Fixed costs ÷ Contribution per unit. Substitution: $420,000 ÷ ($16.00 − $9.00) = $420,000 ÷ $7.00 = 60,000 units. Answer: break-even output is 60,000 units a year.
Formula: Contribution per unit = Selling price − Variable cost per unit. Substitution: $16.00 − $9.00 = $7.00. Answer: contribution per unit is $7.00.

sub_parts.question_text: Explain four ways WLX's management can use this financial data.
sub_parts.model_answer:
1. Comparing the 60,000-unit break-even output with actual output of 74,000 units gives a margin of safety of 14,000 units, confirming the distribution operation is profitable and supporting the $900,000 automation investment.
2. Contribution per unit of $7.00 lets managers model the $0.60 premium from the retailer survey: if granted as a discount instead, contribution would fall to $6.40 and break-even would rise to 65,625 units ($420,000 ÷ $6.40), so extra volume must be won.
3. With fixed costs of $420,000, managers can set the volume needed to service the $600,000 bank loan and check that 74,000 units covers it before further borrowing.
4. Unit cost data ($420,000 ÷ 74,000 units + $9.00 = $14.68 a unit) can be benchmarked monthly to detect the rising 3.6% stock damage and to judge whether the 10.5% energy and packaging rise is being absorbed without eroding contribution.

questions.model_answer: (i) Break-even output = 60,000 units | (ii) Contribution per unit = $7.00 | (iii) Four contextual uses explained: margin of safety of 14,000 units against 74,000 output; discount modelling with $0.60 and $6.40 contribution; loan servicing against $420,000 fixed costs; and unit-cost benchmarking at $14.68 to tackle stock damage.

working_marks: 1 mark for correct formula/method and 1 mark for accurate numerical answer in (i) and (ii). 1 mark per valid applied point in (iii).

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 2, evaluate the profitability of WLX by calculating the gross profit margin, the profit margin and return on capital employed (ROCE) for 2024 and 2025. Has WLX's financial performance improved? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Calculations:
Gross Profit Margin 2024 = 35.0%
Gross Profit Margin 2025 = 40.0%
Profit Margin 2024 = 12.0%
Profit Margin 2025 = 14.0%
ROCE 2024 = 16.0%
ROCE 2025 = 18.0%

Detailed workings: 2024 gross profit of $1,050,000 on revenue of $3,000,000 compares with 2025 gross profit of $1,440,000 on revenue of $3,600,000; cost of sales rose only from $1,950,000 to $2,160,000 while revenue grew faster. Operating profit increased from $360,000 to $504,000, and capital employed from $2,250,000 to $2,800,000; interest payable rose from $50,000 to $72,000, which is still small relative to operating profit.

Evaluation: Every measure moved favourably. The 35.0% to 40.0% change shows WLX kept more of each revenue dollar after direct handling costs, so the 10.5% energy and packaging shock was partly absorbed through the $16.00 price and higher volumes. The 12.0% to 14.0% operating result shows overhead control during expansion, and the 16.0% to 18.0% return on capital employed shows the asset base generated more operating profit even as the $900,000 racking project was funded. The rise in interest payable is gradual and affordable. The main caution is that capital employed grew sharply, so the new automation must earn adequate returns; the 3.6% damage rate and absenteeism also threaten future efficiency.

Conclusion: WLX's financial performance has improved. Gross margin, operating margin and return on capital employed all rose together between 2024 and 2025, indicating broad-based improvement rather than a one-off gain. WLX should proceed with the $900,000 investment while monitoring that new capital earns comparable returns and that stock damage is reduced.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: States financial figures or changes without accurate ratio calculations.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Accurately calculates all three profitability ratios for both 2024 and 2025 with contextual analysis of the trend.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Accurate ratio calculations for both years combined with detailed evaluation of margins, operating profit and capital employed and a justified conclusion on whether performance improved.

questions.question_text: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage for WLX of offering an error-free fulfilment guarantee to its retail clients.
questions.model_answer:
Advantage: The survey of 450 retail managers found 66% would pay up to $0.60 more for error-free fulfilment, so WLX can add a premium that protects its $7.00 contribution per unit even as energy and packaging costs rise 10.5%. It also appeals to the 62% who check stock accuracy before renewing contracts, helping WLX keep existing retail business and win the volume needed to justify the $900,000 racking investment.

Disadvantage: Guaranteeing error-free fulfilment requires extra inspection, skilled staff and reliable systems, which could push up the $420,000 fixed costs and the $9.00 variable cost per unit. With stock damage already at 3.6% and absenteeism rising, any failure would trigger penalties and damage client trust. The $600,000 bank loan leaves limited spare cash to fund a costly guarantee, and retailers may demand it without accepting the full $0.60 premium across all 74,000 units. The $600,000 loan also limits the funds available for the extra inspection staff a guarantee would need.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for a valid advantage and 1 mark for a valid disadvantage.
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual development linked to WLX's survey data, costs and investment.

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the interest rate rise to 4.75%, the 6.0% minimum wage increase and the 10.5% rise in energy and packaging input costs will affect WLX. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Interest rate rise (4.00% to 4.75%): If WLX's $600,000 bank loan is variable-rate, the annual interest cost rises by 0.75% of $600,000 = $4,500 a year (0.0075 × $600,000). That is modest beside fixed costs of $420,000, and if the loan is fixed-rate the increase is zero. Higher rates may also caution retailers and raise the cost of future borrowing, but WLX can largely remove this risk by fixing the loan rate.

Minimum wage increase (6.0%, to $13.78 per hour): WLX employs a workforce of 60 in warehousing, so a wage rise feeds into its cost base and is not optional. The insert gives no hours worked or individual pay, so no defensible annual wage total can be invented; the honest test is productivity — 74,000 units ÷ 60 staff = about 1,233 units per worker. If productivity holds, the rise is affordable; if absenteeism lowers it, unit labour cost rises and the $7.00 contribution per unit is squeezed.

Energy and packaging inputs (10.5%): WLX's variable cost of $9.00 per unit will be affected, but the insert does not decompose it, so only a bound is honest: if the whole variable cost rose 10.5% it would add 10.5% × $9.00 = $0.95 per unit, and at 74,000 units that is about $70,000 a year (74,000 × $0.95). Even a smaller pass-through cuts the $7.00 contribution materially. WLX can offset part through the $0.60 error-free premium in the survey.

Conclusion: The 10.5% energy and packaging rise will have the greatest impact because it compounds across all 74,000 units handled and directly erodes the $7.00 contribution that supports the $900,000 automation. The wage rise is second because it can be managed through productivity; the interest-rate effect is smallest and can be fixed. WLX should secure the $0.60 premium and improve energy efficiency to protect margins.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Identifies the external factors with limited application to WLX.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Analyses the impact of at least two external changes on WLX's costs, revenue or financing in context.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed evaluation of all three external changes in the context of WLX with a well-justified judgment that input costs have the greatest impact and why the other two are smaller.
